content.intro: This lesson covers alignment evaluation through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Study how foundation models are trained and adapted, how human preferences influence alignment, and when prompting or retrieval is more appropriate than fine-tuning.
content.why_it_matters: Treat instruction-following evaluations as part of the model's input contract: state the task, provide only relevant context, specify what a good response looks like, and test representative and ambiguous cases. A prompt can guide behavior, but application code must still validate important outputs.

items.title: Preference agreement
items.text: Use preference agreement as a lens for understanding alignment evaluation. Trace its inputs, the operation or decision it describes, the result a learner can observe, and the limitations that matter for the intended task. Confirm the idea with a small example and an explicit check rather than relying on fluent or plausible output.

items.title: Safety and refusal evaluation
items.text: Safety and refusal evaluation is a control problem as much as a model-behavior problem. Establish explicit boundaries in trusted application code, minimize data exposure, test realistic misuse and failure cases, and record who is responsible for reviewing residual risk. A prompt alone is not a security boundary.

items.title: Robustness and regression testing
items.text: Use robustness and regression testing to turn a vague quality claim into an observable criterion. Define a representative dataset, an expected outcome or rubric, a baseline, and the failure categories you will record; interpret aggregate scores alongside examples and affected groups.

items.title: Understanding alignment limitations
items.text: For understanding alignment limitations, distinguish the training objective from the evaluation goal. Check provenance and data quality, keep validation/test examples isolated from training, record the baseline and configuration, and evaluate both improvement on the target task and possible regressions elsewhere.

content.task: Practice instruction-following evaluations within alignment evaluation: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
